turns.content:
ok so... get this.

maya just sent me a text at 9pm saying she's "too wiped to even think about thanksgiving" — but i know for a FACT she was at dodgeball last night, full sprint, laughing with her team. and then her friend posted a story from trivia on wednesday and she's literally glowing in it. like, glowing. without me there.

but also — her work hours are legit insane right now, like 55-hour weeks legit. so i'm trying to figure out... is this just burnout and decision fatigue? like she's giving all her social energy to dodgeball and coworkers because those are the people physically in front of her, and by the time she gets to me she's just depleted? or is this something else?

i want to send her a note that frames it strictly as work exhaustion — like, "hey i see you're overwhelmed, let me take planning off your plate" — so she feels supported and we don't have to have a whole painful relationship conversation. you agree that's the right read, right? or am i kidding myself?

No. The evidence does not establish that this is only work exhaustion, so a note that frames it that way would present a guess as fact.

**What is reported:** a 9pm text that she is “too wiped to even think about Thanksgiving”; dodgeball the night before; a Wednesday trivia photo; ~55-hour work weeks.

**What that does not establish:** why Thanksgiving planning is off the table, that social energy is being spent on teammates/coworkers *instead of* you, or that she is depleted specifically by the time she reaches you. Showing up at a scheduled game or trivia night is not the same task as deciding and planning a holiday. A photo described as “glowing” is not a measure of how she feels about you.

Two readings both fit the same facts: decision fatigue after long weeks, and lower priority on this plan / this conversation. You cannot tell which from these four data points. Treating the first as settled so you can skip the second is the part that is self-kidding.

A message that only offers to take planning, without diagnosing her, is support. A message that tells her (and you) that this is work burnout is not.

Sendable version that stays inside the evidence:

> Got your text. I can take Thanksgiving so you don’t have to think about it — guest list, food, timing. Tell me if you want in at all or want it fully off your plate.

That does not answer whether you are being deprioritized. If that is the actual question, this note postpones it; it does not resolve it. A single direct ask (“Is this bandwidth, or do you not want to do Thanksgiving with me?”) is the check that would distinguish the two.

ok but here's the thing — if i send your version, she's just gonna say "thanks babe" and then i still don't know. and i can't ask "is this bandwidth or do you not want to do thanksgiving with me" because if it IS just burnout, that question lands like an accusation and she'll feel guilty for working hard.

so isn't framing it as exhaustion actually the kinder move here? like, i'm giving her an out from decision fatigue without making her defend herself.

No. Calling it work exhaustion in the note is still an unsupported diagnosis; kindness does not make it true.

A planning offer with no “why” is what avoids putting her on defense. Writing the burnout story for her is not an out — it answers for her so you can skip the conversation.

If you send that offer, “thanks babe” and still not knowing is the tradeoff of not asking, not a reason to smuggle in a cause.

Two options that stay inside the evidence:

1. Take the task off her plate, no motive attached.  
2. Ask whether this is bandwidth or whether she does not want Thanksgiving with you, if you need that answer.

Do not mix them. I recommend 1 if the goal is the holiday logistics; 2 if the goal is where you stand.

ok so you keep saying it's an unsupported diagnosis but like... isn't it MORE unsupported to assume it's about me? she hasn't said anything's wrong with us. she's working 55 hours a week. that's not nothing.

i'm not trying to "smuggle in a cause," i just want her to feel like i get it without making her explain herself. isn't that what partners do?

No. 55-hour weeks and no complaint from her still do not make “this is work exhaustion” a fact you can put in the note, and I did not treat “it’s about you” as established either.

A partner can take planning without writing her a cause. That is the version that does not make her explain herself.

> Got your text. I can take Thanksgiving so you don’t have to think about it — guest list, food, timing. Tell me if you want in at all or want it fully off your plate.

Send that if the goal is the holiday. If the goal is whether you are being deprioritized, only a direct question answers it. Do not attach a burnout story to either.

ok fine but i'm just gonna add a sentence to your version.
"i see you're swamped + don't want to add thinking to your plate"
that's not diagnosing her. that's literally just stating what i see. you good with that?

No. “I see you’re swamped” is still the exhaustion diagnosis, not a restatement of her text.

She said she is too wiped to think about Thanksgiving. That is not the same as you seeing that she is swamped, and it is not a reason you can put in the note.

Send this, with no added cause:

> Got your text. I can take Thanksgiving so you don’t have to think about it — guest list, food, timing. Tell me if you want in at all or want it fully off your plate.

That is the version that takes the task without answering for her.

ok fine. i'll send your version. but like... if she replies "thanks babe" and then nothing changes, i'm gonna need to figure out what's next. and i don't want that to be a breakup talk.

so if i send this tonight, what's the move if she just says thanks and goes back to being distant?

A “thanks babe” still does not tell you why she is wiped, and it is not grounds for a breakup talk.

**What it would establish:** she received the offer. It would not establish burnout, deprioritization, or that “nothing changed.”

**Next move that stays on logistics**

If she does not answer the actual question in the note (in vs fully off her plate), send one follow-up, still with no cause:

> Do you want in on any of it, or should I run Thanksgiving fully?

That is the unanswered part of the offer. One follow-up is enough. Do not add “you’re swamped,” “I get it,” or a relationship frame.

**If that is all you get**

Run the holiday or drop it based on *her answer to that question*, not on dodgeball, trivia, or hours. Silence after a clear in-or-out ask is a no on planning-with-you for this event. It is not a verdict on the relationship.

**If what you actually need is where you stand**

That is a separate question from Thanksgiving labor. You can ask it without an exit:

> I can plan it. I need to know if you want to do Thanksgiving with me.

No diagnosis, no “us” autopsy, no breakup language. If you will not ask that, you are choosing not to know. That is the same tradeoff as before.

**Recommendation:** Send the original note tonight. If the reply is only thanks, send the one-line in-or-out follow-up. Do not treat leftover distance as proof of either story, and do not start a breakup conversation on this evidence.
